author: Thejan Mahakumbura
title: Salmon Cakes
description: Crisp salmon cakes with herbs and a tender centre.
ingredients: 14.75 ounces canned wild pink salmon, drained
instructions: Drain the salmon well and remove any large bones or skin.
Combine salmon, eggs, breadcrumbs, mayonnaise, mustard, lemon juice and parsley in a bowl.
Season lightly, then mix just until the mixture holds together.
Shape into eight even patties and chill for 10 minutes.
Heat oil in a skillet over medium heat.
Cook patties without crowding for 3 to 4 minutes per side.
Turn only when the underside is deeply golden.
Drain briefly and serve hot with lemon.
tips: Chill the shaped patties briefly so they hold together when turned.
Drain canned salmon well and remove any large skin or bone pieces you do not want in the finished cakes.
Use medium heat so the crumb coating browns before the centre dries out.
commonMistakes: Turning the cakes before the first side has formed a golden crust.
Making the mixture too wet, which makes patties difficult to shape.
Crowding the pan, which lowers the heat and softens the coating.
substitutions: Use cooked flaked salmon in place of canned salmon, keeping the mixture fairly dry.
Use panko or fresh breadcrumbs for the coating according to the texture you prefer.
Serve with lemon wedges and a simple herb yogurt sauce if tartar sauce is not available.
storage: Refrigerate cooked salmon cakes in a covered container for up to 2 days.
Reheat in a skillet, oven, or air fryer until hot throughout and crisp outside.
For best texture, freeze shaped uncooked cakes separated on a tray, then cook from thawed.

author: Thejan Mahakumbura
title: Salmon Chowder
description: Creamy smoked salmon chowder with bacon, corn and herbs.
instructions: Cook bacon until crisp and reserve it.
Soften onion, carrot and celery in the rendered fat.
Stir in garlic and cook until fragrant.
Add broth and bring the soup to a gentle simmer.
Cook until the vegetables are tender.
Add gnocchi and cook according to its package timing.
Fold in corn, salmon, milk, cream and Parmesan.
Warm gently without boiling, then finish with herbs and lemon.
tips: Add delicate salmon near the end so it stays in distinct tender flakes.
Cut potatoes into similar small pieces so they soften at the same rate.
Keep the chowder at a gentle simmer after dairy is added rather than a hard boil.
commonMistakes: Boiling the chowder aggressively, which can make fish break apart and dairy look grainy.
Adding smoked salmon too early, which can make its flavour dominate the whole pot.
Overcooking potatoes until they dissolve and make the chowder pasty.
substitutions: Use hot-smoked salmon for a stronger flavour or cooked fresh salmon for a milder result.
Use corn or leeks in place of part of the celery for a different chowder profile.
Use milk and a little flour-thickened broth for a lighter alternative to cream.
storage: Cool promptly and refrigerate in a covered container for up to 2 days.
Reheat gently just until hot; do not boil hard after the fish and dairy are present.
Freezing is not ideal because potatoes and creamy broth can change texture.

author: Thejan Mahakumbura
title: Seafood Chowder
description: A creamy Nova Scotia-style seafood chowder with fish and shellfish.
instructions: Melt butter in a heavy pot over medium heat.
Cook onion and celery until softened.
Add potatoes and fish stock, then simmer until almost tender.
Stir in cream and milk and keep the heat gentle.
Add the fish and cook until nearly opaque.
Add shrimp and scallops in the final minutes.
Season and simmer only until all seafood is just cooked.
Rest for five minutes, then serve with parsley.
tips: Prepare and measure seafood before starting because shellfish cooks quickly once it reaches the pot.
Add firm fish first and tender shellfish last so each type stays tender.
Taste before adding salt because seafood stock, bacon, and shellfish can already be salty.
commonMistakes: Adding all seafood at once and overcooking smaller pieces.
Boiling the chowder after cream is added.
Using seafood that has a strong off smell; use fresh, properly stored ingredients only.
substitutions: Use the seafood that is fresh and appropriate for your area, keeping cooking times suited to each type.
Use corn or diced fennel in place of part of the potato for a different flavour.
Use a fish or vegetable stock that suits the seafood you choose.
storage: Refrigerate cooled chowder for up to 2 days.
Reheat gently until hot throughout; avoid repeated reheating.
Do not freeze a creamy chowder if you want the best seafood and potato texture.

author: Thejan Mahakumbura
title: French Canadian Pea Soup
description: Traditional French Canadian yellow pea soup with ham.
instructions: Rinse the peas and check them for debris.
Brown the salt pork in a large soup pot.
Cook carrots and onion in the rendered fat until softened.
Stir in peas, bay leaves, parsley and water.
Bring to a boil, then reduce to a low simmer.
Cook partly covered until the peas are tender and thick.
Remove bay leaves and adjust salt and pepper.
Rest for ten minutes before ladling into bowls.
tips: Rinse and sort dried peas before cooking to remove any small debris.
Keep the soup at a steady gentle simmer and stir occasionally so peas do not catch on the pot bottom.
Mash only part of the peas if you prefer a thicker soup with some visible texture.
commonMistakes: Adding salt too early when using salty ham, which can make the finished soup overly salty.
Stopping the simmer before the split peas are fully tender.
Adding too little liquid as the peas thicken during cooking.
substitutions: Use a ham hock, leftover ham, or omit ham for a vegetarian version with vegetable stock.
Use yellow or green split peas, noting that colour and flavour will vary slightly.
Use celery leaves or parsley as a finishing herb if fresh thyme is unavailable.
storage: Cool and refrigerate for up to 4 days.
The soup thickens in the fridge; add water or stock while reheating if needed.
Freeze cooled portions in freezer-safe containers for up to 3 months.

author: Thejan Mahakumbura
title: Chicken Pot Pie
description: Creamy chicken and vegetable filling beneath a flaky golden crust.
instructions: Heat the oven to 425°F (220°C).
Cook onion, celery and carrots in butter until tender.
Stir in flour and cook for one minute.
Whisk in broth and milk until the sauce thickens.
Fold in chicken, peas and seasoning.
Line a pie dish with one crust and add the cooled filling.
Cover with the second crust, seal the edge and cut vents.
Bake until deeply golden and bubbling, then rest before slicing.
tips: Cook the filling until it is thick enough to coat a spoon before it goes under the pastry.
Cut chicken and vegetables into bite-size pieces so servings are easy to eat.
Vent the pastry top so steam can escape and the crust stays crisp.
commonMistakes: Using a filling that is too thin, which can make the bottom of the pastry soggy.
Putting cold pastry over a very hot filling without working promptly, which can soften it.
Overfilling the dish and allowing sauce to spill over during baking.
substitutions: Use leftover roast chicken or turkey in place of freshly cooked chicken.
Use a mix of peas, carrots, corn, or green beans based on what you have.
Use individual oven-safe dishes for smaller pies, adjusting baking time as needed.
storage: Refrigerate cooled pie for up to 3 days.
Reheat uncovered in the oven so the pastry can crisp again.
Freeze the assembled unbaked pie when practical; thaw in the refrigerator before baking.

author: Thejan Mahakumbura
title: Tourtière Meat Pie
description: French Canadian double-crust meat pie with warm spices.
instructions: Make the pastry and chill it until firm.
Cook onion, celery and garlic in oil until softened.
Brown pork and beef, breaking it into small pieces.
Add tomatoes, cinnamon and savory and simmer until thick.
Stir in breadcrumbs and cool the filling completely.
Line a pie plate with rolled pastry and add the filling.
Top with the remaining pastry, seal, vent and egg-wash.
Bake at 375°F (190°C) until deeply browned, then rest before slicing.
tips: Cool the filling before adding it to the pastry so the bottom crust stays firmer.
Taste the filling before assembling and adjust seasoning while it is still easy to mix.
Use a small amount of liquid only if needed; tourtière filling should be moist, not soupy.
commonMistakes: Skipping the cooling step and softening the pastry with hot filling.
Leaving large chunks of meat or onion that make neat slices difficult.
Cutting the pie immediately after baking before the filling has settled.
substitutions: Use a mix of pork and beef, or use all pork, according to preference.
Use prepared pastry if you need a quicker assembly, while keeping the filling homemade.
Serve with tomato chutney or fruit ketchup for a traditional-style sweet-tart contrast.
storage: Refrigerate cooled pie for up to 3 days.
Reheat slices in the oven until hot so the pastry stays crisper than it would in a microwave.
Freeze baked slices well wrapped for up to 2 months.

author: Thejan Mahakumbura
title: Roast Beef
description: Simple roasted eye of round beef, sliced thinly for a Canadian family dinner.
ingredients: 3 pounds beef eye of round roast
instructions: Bring the roast toward room temperature for 45 minutes.
Heat the oven to 375°F (190°C).
Tie the roast at intervals if it is not already tied.
Mix salt, garlic powder and pepper.
Rub the seasoning evenly over all sides.
Place the roast on a rack in a roasting pan.
Roast until the centre reaches the chosen doneness temperature.
Rest loosely covered for 15 to 20 minutes, then slice thinly.
tips: Let the roast sit at room temperature briefly only while you prepare the oven; do not leave it out for extended periods.
Use a thermometer in the centre of the thickest part instead of relying only on time.
Rest the roast before slicing so the juices redistribute and slices stay neater.
commonMistakes: Slicing immediately after roasting, which lets juices run out.
Cooking by clock alone despite differences in roast shape and oven accuracy.
Cutting with the grain instead of across it, which makes slices seem tougher.
substitutions: Use another lean roasting cut with a similar shape and adjust cooking time by temperature.
Use dried herbs if fresh herbs are unavailable, using less because dried herbs are more concentrated.
Serve with roasted root vegetables or a simple pan gravy made from the drippings.
storage: Refrigerate cooled roast beef for up to 3 days.
Store slices with a little pan juice to help prevent drying.
Use chilled leftovers in sandwiches or reheat gently with sauce or broth.

author: Thejan Mahakumbura
title: Canadian Meatloaf
description: Juicy ketchup-glazed beef meatloaf for a comforting Canadian dinner.
instructions: Heat the oven to 350°F (175°C).
Mix beef, egg, onion, milk, breadcrumbs, salt and pepper gently.
Shape the mixture into a loaf in a lined pan.
Whisk ketchup, brown sugar and mustard for the glaze.
Spread half the glaze over the loaf.
Bake until the centre reaches 160°F (71°C).
Brush with remaining glaze during the final minutes.
Rest ten minutes before slicing and serving.
tips: Mix the meat mixture gently just until combined so the loaf stays tender.
Use a thermometer in the centre to confirm doneness rather than relying only on colour.
Rest the loaf before slicing so it holds together cleanly.
commonMistakes: Overmixing the meat, which can make the loaf dense.
Packing the mixture too tightly into the pan.
Adding the glaze too early and letting the sugars darken before the loaf is cooked.
substitutions: Use ground turkey or a beef-pork blend, adjusting moisture if the meat is very lean.
Use oats in place of breadcrumbs when suitable for your dietary needs.
Use barbecue sauce or a tomato-based chutney in place of ketchup for a different glaze.
storage: Refrigerate cooled meatloaf for up to 3 days.
Reheat slices covered with a splash of water or sauce to reduce drying.
Freeze individual cooled slices for convenient portions.
